Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Hay-Zama Wood Bison Aerial Survey (2023) 
Background 
The Hay-Zama wood bison population (Bison bison athabascae) was established through introducing wood bison as part of 
national efforts to recover wood bison populations and the establishment of freeranging, self-sustaining and disease-free wood 
bison in each of the provinces and territories in Western Canada. The Hay-Zama population is managed by a regulated 
hunting season to achieve a population objective between 400 and 600 animals. This ensures a sustainable population while 
also limiting bison distribution toward Highway 35 and reducing potential contact with diseased bison to the east, in and 
around Wood Buffalo National Park. A minimum total count is conducted annually in late February or March. All bison found 
are counted and classified as adult or calf to determine the herd composition. 
For more information about management of the Hay-Zama Wood Bison herd and issues of diseased bison in Alberta, readers 
can link to: 
• https://mywildalberta.ca/hunting/game-species/wood-bison-hunt-hay-zama.aspx   
• https://www.alberta.ca/wood-bison-disease-management.aspx?utm_source=redirector 
Survey Method 
The 2023 Hay-Zama bison survey was conducted by flying transects orientated east-west and spaced one degree of latitude 
apart (roughly one statue mile) within the historical range. The search area was expanded slightly to the North to cover areas 
of known bison occupancy. The crew consisted of 2 to 3 observers in a Bell 206 Jet Ranger equipped with bubble windows in 
the rear. Survey speed was approximately 90 to 110 km per hour. All groups were photographed to confirm total counts and 
classification of adults and calves. The adult classification includes juveniles and both sexes due to the difficulty in accurately 
separating between sex and age classes. Calves were classified based on relatively small size and shorter nasal bridge. 
Results and Discussion 
The Hay-Zama bison survey was undertaken from February 23-March 1, 2023. A total of 529 bison (448 adults and 81 calves) 
were seen in 45 groups. There was 15 percent calves, consistent with the previous 5-year average.
